definition: How the mean $\bar{X}$ of a random sample of size $n$ varies from sample to sample: it has mean $\mu$ and variance $\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}$ (the variance, not the standard deviation, is divided by $n$), and it is exactly $\mathrm{N}\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}\right)$ when the population is $\mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^{2})$.

The result that the mean $\bar{X}$ of a random sample of size $n$ from any population with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$ is approximately $\mathrm{N}\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}\right)$ when $n$ is large, where how large depends on the population and IB exams treat $n > 30$ as enough.
